pool.prompt: A fiber project requires crossing a navigable river with an HDD bore. Which federal permit authorizes this work?
choices: FCC 47 CFR 1.1411 — pole attachment authorization

USACE Nationwide Permit 57 (NWP 57, "Electric Utility Line and Telecommunications Activities") — pre-authorizes telecommunications line crossings of waters of the US, including fiber conduit HDD bores
NESC — underground crossing clearances
7 CFR 1753.49 — closeout documentation authorization
pool.explanation: The US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) regulates navigable waters and wetlands under the Clean Water Act / Rivers and Harbors Act. NWP 57 specifically covers electric utility line and telecommunications activities, pre-authorizing fiber HDD crossings subject to conditions (utility-line activities were split out of the former NWP 12, which now covers only oil/gas pipelines).
pool.citation: USACE Nationwide Permit 57, Electric Utility Line and Telecommunications Activities (2021 reissuance).

pool.prompt: A splicer on an RUS-funded project is told the cable must be "RUS-listed." What does this mean in practice?
choices: The cable must be manufactured in the United States
The cable must appear on RUS's accepted materials list, governed under 7 CFR Part 1755 (Telecommunications Policies on Specifications, Acceptable Materials, and Standard Contract Forms)
The cable must be labeled with the RUS logo on the outer jacket
The cable must be the lowest-cost option that meets TIA specifications
pool.explanation: RUS maintains accepted-materials requirements for funded projects under 7 CFR Part 1755. Cable not on the accepted list generally cannot be used on a funded project without specific RUS approval. (RUS Bulletin 1753F-201 is a distinct bulletin covering acceptance TESTING of completed telecommunications plant — not the materials-acceptance list itself; do not conflate the two.)
pool.citation: 7 CFR Part 1755 (Telecommunications Policies on Specifications, Acceptable Materials, and Standard Contract Forms); RUS Bulletin 1753F-201 correctly identified as "Acceptance Tests and Measurements of Telecommunications Plant" — see T01.md research log for this correction.

pool.prompt: Which international standards body publishes the G.652 (standard single-mode fiber) and G.657 (bend-insensitive single-mode fiber) optical performance specifications?
choices: ANSI
ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union — Telecommunication Standardization Sector)
BICSI
ICEA
pool.explanation: The ITU-T (a UN specialized agency) publishes the G-series recommendations governing optical fiber performance. G.652.D is the dominant standard for OSP single-mode fiber; G.657.A1/A2 are bend-insensitive variants used for tight-bend drop applications.

pool.prompt: When NESC and an applicable RUS engineering bulletin specify different requirements for the same design element on an RUS-funded project, which generally governs?
choices: NESC always supersedes RUS bulletins
The RUS bulletin always supersedes NESC
The more stringent requirement governs — both function as floors, not ceilings; apply whichever standard is stricter for that element and document the rationale
The designer chooses whichever standard is cheaper to implement
pool.explanation: NESC compliance is required by state utility regulations; RUS bulletin compliance is a loan condition for funded projects. Neither displaces the other — where they differ, the more stringent requirement applies, and a design meeting both is the only acceptable outcome.

pool.prompt: How does a privately-published standard (e.g., an IEEE or NFPA document) become legally enforceable?
choices: It is automatically federal law the moment it is published
A government body (state legislature, public utility commission, or local jurisdiction) must adopt it by reference in law or regulation — until adopted, it is voluntary
It becomes enforceable only after the FCC issues a rulemaking specifically for that standard
Standards from professional organizations can never become legally enforceable
pool.explanation: Standards from bodies like IEEE, NFPA, and TIA are written by industry committees but are voluntary until a government body adopts them by reference into law or regulation — for example, a state public utility commission adopting NESC. Different jurisdictions may adopt different editions, which is why designers must confirm the specific adopted edition for a given project location.

pool.prompt: What is the primary role of ICEA (Insulated Cable Engineers Association) in the OSP standards landscape?
choices: It is a federal regulatory agency enforcing cable safety law

It publishes cable construction standards (e.g., ICEA S-87-640 for OSP fiber cable) that define how cable is built and what environmental performance it must meet — widely cited in cable specifications though not itself a regulatory body
It licenses individual splicers and OSP designers
It replaces TIA for all fiber-related standards
pool.explanation: ICEA is a non-regulatory industry standards organization. Its cable-construction standards, like S-87-640 for OSP fiber cable, are widely referenced in procurement specs and by RUS materials-acceptance requirements, but ICEA itself has no enforcement authority.

pool.prompt: What does "47 CFR" refer to, and which federal telecom rules live there?
choices: Title 47 of the Code of Federal Regulations — where FCC rules live, including pole attachment timelines/rates (Part 1) and other telecommunications regulation
A specific RUS engineering bulletin series
The 47th edition of the National Electrical Safety Code
A USACE permit designation for underwater crossings
pool.explanation: CFR = Code of Federal Regulations, organized by title. Title 47 covers Telecommunications and is where FCC rules live (e.g., Part 1 pole-attachment rules). Different agencies' rules live in different CFR titles: 7 CFR for USDA/RUS, 29 CFR for OSHA, 33 CFR for the Army Corps of Engineers.

pool.prompt: Match each standards body to what it governs in OSP work.

items.label: Aerial line clearances, loading, attachment heights (NESC/C2)
Building electrical installation, grounding, indoor cable ratings (NEC/NFPA 70)
Optical fiber performance specs (G.652, G.657, G.984)
Cable construction standards (e.g., S-87-640 for OSP fiber cable)

pool.explanation: IEEE publishes NESC (aerial line code); NFPA publishes NEC (building electrical code); ITU-T publishes the G-series optical fiber performance recommendations; ICEA publishes cable construction/qualification standards. All four apply to different aspects of the same OSP project simultaneously.
